meta.title: S1 · Les 51 — ‘Hebben’ or ‘zijn’ in the present perfect
meta.subtitle: Lesson 51 – ‘Hebben’ or ‘zijn’ in the present perfect

sentences.nl: Mijn naam is Bart de Pau,, online docent Nederlands.
sentences.en: My name is Bart de Pau, online Dutch teacher.

sentences.nl: Vandaag oefenen we Nederlandse zinnen, met de grammatica van #dutchgrammar-2 les 26 en 27.
sentences.en: Today we practice Dutch sentences, with the grammar from #dutchgrammar-2 lesson 26 and 27.

sentences.nl: In die lessen ik uit, of je ‘hebben’ of ‘zijn’ moet gebruiken in het perfectum.
sentences.en: In those lessons I explain whether you should use 'have' or 'be' in the perfect tense.

sentences.nl: Voor veel studenten is dit erg moeilijk.
sentences.en: This is very difficult for many students.

sentences.nl: Daarom is het belangrijk dat we dit veel oefenen.
sentences.en: That is why it is important that we practice this a lot.

sentences.nl: Niet alleen in deze aflevering,, maar ook in de volgende afleveringen.
sentences.en: Not only in this episode, but also in the following episodes.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Not only in this episode, but also in the next episodes.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Niet alleen... maar ook" is a common structure used to connect two related ideas, similar to "not only... but also" in English.  
• "In deze aflevering" uses "in" as a preposition, which is used similarly to English.  
• "De volgende afleveringen" uses "de" as the definite article and "volgende" to indicate "next" or "following".

Extra phrases/sentences:  
• "Niet alleen zij, maar ook hij wil gaan." (Not only she, but also he wants to go.)  
• "Niet alleen vandaag, maar ook morgen regent het." (Not only today, but also tomorrow it will rain.)  
• "Niet alleen kinderen, maar ook volwassenen houden van spelletjes." (Not only children, but also adults love games.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Niet alleen de film, maar ook het boek was spannend." (Not only the movie, but also the book was exciting.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• No specific cultural note applies in this context.

sentences.nl: Soliman en Xing, zijn wat eerder naar het klaslokaal gekomen.

sentences.nl: Ze zitten te praten.
sentences.en: They are talking.

sentences.nl: Soliman zegt tegen Xing:, Gisteravond heb ik een rondje gelopen.
sentences.en: Soliman says to Xing, "Last night I went for a walk."
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Soliman says to Xing: "Last night have I a round walked."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Zegt tegen" means "says to," where "tegen" is a preposition used with "zeggen" to indicate to whom something is being said.  
• "Gisteravond" is a compound noun meaning "last night." It is made up of "gister" (yesterday) and "avond" (evening).  
• The phrase "heb ik een rondje gelopen" is in the present perfect tense, which is often used in Dutch to describe past actions. The auxiliary verb "heb" (have) is used with the past participle "gelopen" (walked).

Extra phrases:  
• "Hij zegt tegen zijn moeder dat hij honger heeft." (He says to his mother that he is hungry.)  
• "Vanmiddag heb ik een boek gelezen." (This afternoon I have read a book.)  
• "Zij heeft gisteren de hele dag gewerkt." (She has worked the whole day yesterday.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Maria zegt tegen Tom: 'Ik heb het nieuwe restaurant geprobeerd.'" (Maria says to Tom: "I have tried the new restaurant.")

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, taking a "rondje lopen" (going for a walk) is a common activity for relaxation and social interaction, often done in the evening or during leisure time.

sentences.nl: Toen zag ik Marieke en Gianluca romantisch dineren.
sentences.en: Then I saw Marieke and Gianluca dining romantically.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Then saw I Marieke and Gianluca romantically dining.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Toen" is used to indicate a specific point in time in the past.  
• The past tense is used here with "zag ik" (saw I) following the word order for past simple sentences.  
• "Romantisch dineren" combines an adverb with an infinitive verb to describe the manner of dining.

Examples:  
– Toen hoorde ik de muziek spelen. (Then I heard the music playing.)  
– Toen begon het te regenen. (Then it started to rain.)  
– Romantisch wandelen langs het strand is heerlijk. (Romantically walking along the beach is lovely.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Toen ontmoette ik mijn oude vriend op het station. (Then I met my old friend at the station.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, dining out romantically is quite common, and restaurants often cater to such experiences with special menus or settings, especially on occasions like Valentine's Day.

sentences.nl: Xing zegt: ‘Ik heb het ook gezien.’
sentences.en: Xing says: 'I saw it too.'

sentences.nl: Ze aten pizza.
sentences.en: They ate pizza.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• They ate pizza.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Ze" is the subject pronoun meaning "they."  
• "Aten" is the past tense of the verb "eten" (to eat). Dutch often forms the past tense by changing the vowel of the verb stem, known as a strong verb.  
• "Pizza" is a direct object, and like in English, it follows the verb.  

Extra phrases:  
- "Ze dronken koffie." (They drank coffee.)  
- "Zij maakten muziek." (They made music.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Ze schreven een brief." (They wrote a letter.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Pizza is a popular food in the Netherlands, similar to many Western countries, and is often eaten in casual settings or as a quick meal option.

sentences.nl: En op die pizza stond een hartje.
sentences.en: And on that pizza was a little heart.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• And on that pizza stood a little heart.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses "En op die pizza" to start with a prepositional phrase, which is common for emphasis or setting the scene in Dutch.  
• "Stond" is the past tense of "staan" (to stand), used here to describe something being on a surface, which is a common Dutch idiom.  
• "Hartje" is the diminutive form of "hart" (heart), commonly used to express smallness or endearment.

Examples:  
• "Op de tafel stond een vaas." (On the table stood a vase.)  
• "In de tuin bloeide een roosje." (In the garden bloomed a little rose.)  
• "Aan de muur hing een schilderijtje." (On the wall hung a small painting.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Op het strand lag een schelpje." (On the beach lay a little shell.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Pizza with unique or personal toppings, such as a heart-shaped topping, can be popular in the Netherlands, especially for celebrations or special occasions.

sentences.nl: Ja, ik weet het.
sentences.en: Yes, I know it.

sentences.nl: Is dat niet een beetje raar? — Marieke zit bij een andere man,, terwijl ze met Martin gaat trouwen.
sentences.en: Isn't that a little strange? — Marieke is with another man, while she's going to marry Martin.

sentences.nl: Daarom ben ik maar niet naar hun toe gegaan.
sentences.en: That's why I just didn't go to them.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Therefore am I just not to them toward gone.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Daarom" is a conjunction meaning "therefore" or "that's why," often used to explain a reason for an action.  
• "Maar" in this context is used to soften the statement, meaning "just" or "only."  
• "Naar hun toe" is a phrase meaning "to them," where "naar" is a preposition and "toe" indicates direction towards a person or place.  
• "Gaan" is the past participle "gegaan," used with the auxiliary verb "ben" to form the present perfect tense.

Examples:  
– "Daarom heb ik het boek gekocht." (That's why I bought the book.)  
– "Ik ben maar even naar buiten gegaan." (I just went outside for a moment.)  
– "Ze is niet naar hem toe gegaan." (She did not go to him.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Daarom heb ik maar niets gezegd. (That's why I just didn't say anything.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• No culture note.

sentences.nl: Op dat moment komt Lars binnen…
sentences.en: At that moment, Lars comes in…

sentences.nl: Hij is verliefd, niet verloofd.

sentences.nl: Soliman, wat betekent dat ‘verliefd’? — ‘Verliefd’… eh… dat woord heb ik geleerd.
sentences.en: Soliman, what does ‘in love’ mean? — ‘In love’... uh... I learned that word.

sentences.nl: Oh ja, dat is als je gaat trouwen.
sentences.en: Oh yes, that's when you get married.

sentences.nl: Oeps… foutje…
sentences.en: Oops… little mistake…
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Oops... little mistake...

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Oeps" is an interjection used to express a minor error or surprise, similar to "oops" in English.  
• "Foutje" is a diminutive form of "fout," which means "mistake" or "error." In Dutch, the diminutive form often softens the tone or conveys something small or minor.  
• The ellipsis ("...") implies continuation or an unfinished thought, often used informally to suggest that more could be said.

– Example 1: "Foutje, bedankt!" (Small mistake, thanks!)—A casual way to acknowledge an error and move on.  
– Example 2: "Kopje koffie?" (Cup of coffee?)—Using the diminutive "kopje" to make the offer sound more casual and friendly.

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Oeps, ik vergat mijn sleutel!" (Oops, I forgot my key!)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The use of diminutives is very common in Dutch and can convey friendliness, informality, or make something sound less serious.

sentences.nl: Martin is gisteravond, al op het vakantiepark aangekomen.
sentences.en: Martin arrived at the holiday park already last night.

sentences.nl: Hij is vannacht gebleven.
sentences.en: He stayed the night.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• He is tonight stayed.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence is in the past tense. "Is gebleven" is the present perfect tense, which is formed using the auxiliary verb "is" (to be) and the past participle "gebleven" (stayed).  
• "Vannacht" means "tonight" but in the sense of the night that just passed.  
• Word order: Subject (Hij) + Auxiliary Verb (is) + Time (vannacht) + Past Participle (gebleven).  
• Examples:  
  - "Zij is gisteren gekomen." (She came yesterday.)  
  - "Wij zijn naar het park geweest." (We went to the park.)  
  - "Jullie zijn laat aangekomen." (You all arrived late.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Zij is vanochtend vertrokken." (She left this morning.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch, the use of "is" as an auxiliary verb in the perfect tense indicates a movement or change of state, often used with verbs like "komen" (to come), "gaan" (to go), and "blijven" (to stay).

sentences.nl: Hij heeft bij mij op de kamer geslapen.
sentences.en: He slept in my room.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• He has by me in the room slept.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The verb "heeft" is an auxiliary verb used to form the perfect tense in Dutch.  
• "Bij mij" means "at my place" or "with me" and indicates location or association.  
• The phrase "op de kamer" means "in the room." The preposition "op" is used here to denote location.  
• Word order: In perfect tense, the past participle ("geslapen") goes to the end of the sentence.

Examples:  
• Zij heeft bij ons gegeten. (She has eaten with us.)  
• Ik heb op de bank gezeten. (I have sat on the couch.)  
• Wij hebben in het park gewandeld. (We have walked in the park.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Hij heeft bij zijn tante gelogeerd. (He has stayed with his aunt.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, it's common for friends to stay over at each other's houses, especially among young people and students. This sentence might be used when explaining past social activities or arrangements.

sentences.nl: En? — Heeft hij nog iets gezegd? — Ik heb niet met hem gesproken, want hij was erg laat.
sentences.en: And? — Did he say anything else? — I didn't speak to him because he was very late.

sentences.nl: Maar volgens mij was hij heel vrolijk.
sentences.en: But I think he was very cheerful.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• But according to me was he very cheerful.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Maar" is a conjunction meaning "but," often used to introduce a contrasting statement.  
• "Volgens mij" translates to "according to me," which is a way to express one's opinion. It's like saying "in my opinion."  
• "Was" is the past tense of "is" (to be).  
• "Hij" is the pronoun for "he."  
• "Heel" means "very," used for emphasis.  
• "Vrolijk" means "cheerful" or "happy."

Examples:  
- Volgens mij is het vandaag koud. (According to me, it is cold today.)  
- Hij was heel boos. (He was very angry.)  
- Maar het regende de hele dag. (But it rained the whole day.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Volgens mij was de film erg grappig. (In my opinion, the movie was very funny.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The phrase "volgens mij" is commonly used in Dutch to politely offer one's opinion, often in discussions or to softly introduce a personal viewpoint.

sentences.nl: Dus ik denk, dat hij met Marieke naar het bruggetje is geweest.
sentences.en: So I think that he has been to the little bridge with Marieke.

sentences.nl: Hmm… het wordt een beetje moeilijk voor mij…, dus Marieke heeft met Gianluca gegeten, en daarna is ze met Martin naar het bruggetje gegaan!? — Martin is niet verloofd met Marieke,, maar hij is wel verliefd op Marieke…
sentences.en: Hmm… it’s getting a bit difficult for me…, so Marieke had dinner with Gianluca, and then she went to the little bridge with Martin!? — Martin is not engaged to Marieke, but he is in love with Marieke…

sentences.en: Martin 'was' in love with Marieke...

sentences.nl: Imperfectum.
sentences.en: Imperfect.

sentences.nl: Nu begrijp ik het niet meer.
sentences.en: Now I don't understand it anymore.

sentences.nl: Eh… ik ook niet…
sentences.en: Uh… me neither…

sentences.nl: Wat weet jij Xing? — Wat is er gisteravond gebeurd? — Xing zegt niets, maar ze moet wel blozen…
sentences.en: What do you know Xing? — What happened last night? — Xing says nothing, but she does blush…
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• What know you Xing? — What is there yesterday evening happened? — Xing says nothing, but she must indeed blush...

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Wat weet jij Xing?" uses inversion for emphasis, placing "weet" (know) before "jij" (you) to stress the question.  
• "Wat is er gisteravond gebeurd?" uses "is gebeurd" for the perfect tense, common for past events. "Er" is a placeholder for the subject.  
• "Maar ze moet wel blozen" uses "moet wel" to indicate an unavoidable or expected reaction.

Examples:  
- "Wat lees jij daar?" (What are you reading there?)  
- "Wat is er met je gebeurd?" (What happened to you?)  
- "Hij moet wel lachen." (He can't help but laugh.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Wat doe jij hier zo laat?" (What are you doing here so late?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, directness is common, so questions like "Wat weet jij?" (What do you know?) are typical in conversations to get straightforward answers.

nederlands.spelling: The 'ee' in 'nee' is a long vowel /eː/ and the 'a' in 'lands' is a short vowel /ɑ/.
nederlands.fast: In rapid speech, the final /ts/ in 'nederlands' may be reduced, causing it to blend with following words.

vandaag.spelling: The combination 'aa' in 'vandaag' indicates a long /aː/ sound, typical for Dutch vowels.
vandaag.fast: The final /x/ in 'vandaag' may be softened or dropped in rapid speech, especially if followed by a vowel.

oefenen.spelling: The sequence 'oe' represents a long /uː/ sound.
oefenen.fast: In casual speech, the final /n/ in ‘oefenen’ may be fully assimilated or nasalized before a vowel.

grammatica.spelling: The initial gr- and -a- in 'grammatica' follow the usual Dutch pronunciation rules for similar Greek-origin words.
grammatica.fast: In rapid speech, the final /a/ in 'grammatica' may be pronounced as a schwa [ə] when followed by a word starting with a consonant.

van.spelling: The short vowel /ɑ/ is common in monosyllabic words ending in -n.
van.fast: The final /n/ in ‘van’ is often elided in casual speech, particularly before consonants.

les.spelling: Short /ɛ/ in a closed syllable followed by a voiceless /s/.
les.fast: In rapid speech, the final /s/ in ‘les is’ may become voiceless between vowels, leading to a pronunciation like [lɛsɪs].

die.spelling: In Dutch, the pronoun 'die' is pronounced with a long /i/ sound, which is common for pronouns and demonstratives.
die.fast: In connected speech, 'die' may become a reduced vowel sound, especially in fast speech or informal contexts.

uit.fast: In rapid speech, the diphthong /œyt/ can be slightly reduced to /œt/.

zijn.spelling: The diphthong 'ij' in 'zijn' is pronounced as /ɛi/.
zijn.fast: In fast speech, 'zijn' may reduce to a schwa sound, especially in unstressed positions.

het.spelling: The ‘h’ is often silent in casual speech, making it sound like ‘et’.
het.fast: In rapid speech, the initial /h/ in ‘het’ may be elided, resulting in a pronunciation closer to [ɛt].

dit.spelling: The short vowel /ɪ/ is followed by a voiceless plosive /t/, typical of closed syllables.
dit.fast: In rapid speech, the /t/ in ‘dit is’ can become a flap [ɾ] or be elided entirely.

dat.spelling: Short vowel /ɑ/ in a closed syllable is represented by a single 'a'.
dat.fast: In connected speech, the /d/ in ‘dat is’ may be voiced to a soft [d̪] before the vowel.

niet.spelling: The vowel 'ie' is pronounced as a long /iː/ sound.
niet.fast: In casual speech, the /t/ in 'niet' may become unreleased or assimilate to a following consonant.

aflevering.spelling: The prefix ‘af-’ indicates a separable prefix, showing a clear boundary with the root.
aflevering.fast: The initial /f/ of ‘aflevering’ may assimilate to a voiced [v] in connected speech, especially after voiced sounds.

maar.spelling: The long vowel /aː/ appears in the open syllable.
maar.fast: In fast speech, the /r/ in 'maar ik' may be reduced or assimilated to the following vowel.

ook.spelling: The long vowel /oː/ is indicated by the open syllable followed by a consonant.
ook.fast: In casual speech, the vowel /oː/ can sometimes become shorter before a following consonant.

nog.spelling: The word 'nog' ends in a voiced velar fricative /x/, which is common in Dutch adverbs.
nog.fast: In rapid speech, the final /x/ in ‘nog’ may be devoiced or slightly reduced before a vowel.

wat.spelling: The short vowel /ɑ/ is common in closed syllables.
wat.fast: In connected speech, 'wat' often reduces to /wət/ or even /wə/ before vowels.

naar.spelling: The long vowel /aː/ appears in the open syllable with the consonant ending.
naar.fast: The final /r/ in ‘naar’ can often be a tapped [ɾ] or even silent in casual speech when followed by a word starting with a consonant.

praten.spelling: The long /aː/ in 'praat' is due to the open syllable, maintained in 'praten'.
praten.fast: In rapid speech, the final /t/ in 'praat ik' can be unreleased or assimilated before a vowel.

heb.spelling: Heb is a monosyllabic word with a short vowel /ɛ/ followed by a voiced bilabial plosive /b/.
heb.fast: In rapid speech, the final /b/ in ‘heb ik’ might be pronounced as a flap or even omitted entirely before the following vowel.

een.spelling: The article ‘een’ is pronounced with a long /eː/ to distinguish it from the numeral ‘één’, which has a stressed pronunciation.
een.fast: In rapid speech, ‘een’ may be reduced to a schwa sound /ən/ when it is unstressed.

marieke.spelling: The name Marieke features a schwa /ə/ often found in unstressed syllables.
marieke.fast: In casual speech, the final /ə/ in 'Marieke' might be less pronounced, sounding almost like a short /ə/ or even omitted.

weet.spelling: Open syllable we- indicates a long /eː/ sound.
weet.fast: In rapid speech, final /t/ in ‘weet ik’ may become a glottal stop [ʔ] before a vowel.

bij.spelling: The diphthong /ɛi̯/ is common in Dutch, often spelled with 'ij'.
bij.fast: In fast speech, the diphthong /ɛi̯/ in 'bij' might be slightly reduced, blending smoothly into following words.

martin.spelling: The /ɑ/ in the first syllable is a short vowel due to the closed syllable pattern.
martin.fast: In connected speech, the /n/ at the end of ‘martin’ may assimilate to a nasalized vowel before a following vowel sound.

ben.spelling: Short vowel /ɛ/ in closed syllable with nasal ending.
ben.fast: In rapid speech, 'ben ik' may sound like [bɛnɪk] with reduced vowel.

wel.spelling: The short vowel /ɛ/ is pronounced because the syllable is closed by the consonant /l/.
wel.fast: In connected speech, the /l/ in ‘wel ik’ might become a dark [ɫ] before a vowel.

nee.spelling: The long vowel /eː/ is represented by the single vowel 'e' in an open syllable.
nee.fast: In rapid speech, ‘nee’ may be pronounced more quickly, reducing the length of the vowel.

wij.spelling: The diphthong /ɛi/ is commonly represented by the letters 'ij' in Dutch.
wij.fast: In rapid speech, the diphthong /ɛi/ can be reduced, leading 'wij zijn' to sound like /ʋə zɛin/.

zin.fast: In rapid speech, the final /n/ in ‘zin heb’ may be realized as a nasalized vowel or dropped in informal contexts.

weten.spelling: Open syllable we- shows long /eː/, closed weet shortens to /e/.
weten.fast: Final /t/ in ‘weet ik’ often assimilates to an unreleased [t̚] before the following vowel.

hoe.spelling: The vowel sound /uː/ in 'hoe' is represented by the letters 'oe', a common Dutch spelling for this sound.
hoe.fast: In rapid speech, the /ˈɦuː/ in ‘hoe gaat’ may blend, with the /ɦ/ becoming less pronounced, sounding like /uːɣaːt/.

tot.spelling: The word 'tot' follows the closed syllable pattern, resulting in a short vowel sound /ɔ/.
tot.fast: In connected speech, the final /t/ in 'tot' may become less aspirated or even assimilate with a following consonant.

dan.spelling: Short vowel /ɑ/ in closed syllable, typical for monosyllabic adverbs.
dan.fast: In rapid speech, 'dan ik' may have the /n/ assimilated to [ŋ] before a velar sound.
